question: The application of Regulation (EC) No 1598/2002 in conjunction with Directive 1999/105/EC raises questions about the scope of the assistance provided and the exchange of information between competent authorities.

Article 16(1) of Directive 1999/105/EC provides that Member States ‘shall, by an official control system set up or approved by them, ensure that reproductive material from individual units of approval or lots remains clearly identifiable through the entire process from collection to delivery to the end user’.

Article 1 of Regulation (EC) No 1598/2002 provides that, when reproductive material is moved from one Member State to another, authorities are to provide each other with ‘information’. To this end, a standardised information document is established by the Regulation. 1.
Do the requirements of the Regulation include systematic reporting of all transactions?
To what extent is the transfer of personal data (e.g. name and address of the buyer) permissible or required under these rules?
Is it compatible with EU law to require economic operators to systematically submit delivery documents for all transactions?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2026) The requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1598/20021 systematically cover all movements of forest reproductive material between two Member States.

Based on the principle of lawfulness enshrined in Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (the ‘GDPR’)2 in conjunction with Article 6 (1)(c) and (e) thereof, the processing of personal data shall be based on Union or Member State Law, and be necessary for compliance with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject and/or for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of an official authority vested in the controller.

In the context of the cross-border movement of forest reproductive material, Article 16 of Council Directive 1999/105/EC3 read together with Commission Regulation (EC) No 1598/20024, provides for the administrative cooperation and the exchange of information between the competent authorities of the Member States concerned in order to ensure traceability and the proper application of the legislation in question.

Furthermore, the Annex to Commission Regulation (EC) No 1598/2002 expressly establishes a standardised ‘Information Document’ for movements of forest reproductive material between Member States, including fields relating to the name and address of the supplier and of the receiver.
In that context, this EU legal framework at hand imposes the legal obligation for the exchange of such personal data, thereby complying with the lawfulness requirement under Regulation (EU) 2016/679.

It should nevertheless be recalled that compliance with Regulation (EU) 2016/679 remains the responsibility of the competent authorities of the Member States, acting as controllers within the meaning of Article 4(7) thereof.
